title: Fragment-aware kernel routing and prefill scheduling for paged KV cache
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Goal: Reduce decode tail latency and per-token cost for long-context workloads by making kernel selection and prefill/ decode scheduling aware of KV page fragmentation and reuse likelihood. This ticket coordinates a runtime change to (1) score KV pages/fragments by reuse probability, (2) route attention kernels based on contiguous fragment layout to avoid many small kernel launches, and (3) prioritize prefill prefetching for fragments with high reuse scores while applying a lightweight, locality-preserving eviction policy.

Background: Our paged KV implementation currently treats pages roughly equally: allocation is first-fit, eviction is LRU on a per-page basis, and kernel selection for attention ops is agnostic to how keys/values are distributed across pages. This causes two observable problems: (a) decode step latency increases when attention must touch many small, non-contiguous fragments resulting in poor kernel utilization and many kernel launches; (b) repeated re-population of recently-used logical KV entries across different pages leads to unnecessary memory traffic and repeated quant/dequant overhead on some formats.

Proposal: Implement a three-part feature set: 
1) Fragment Reuse Scoring: maintain a lightweight per-fragment score (history window ~512 requests) computed from access frequency, recency, and cost-to-repopulate estimate. Score updates are approximate (exponential decay counters) to keep CPU overhead <1% of runtime.
2) Fragment-aware Kernel Routing: extend the kernel selector to prefer kernels that operate on larger contiguous physical ranges when the majority of active attention keys fall inside N contiguous pages (configurable threshold). Fall back to small-fragment kernels when distribution is highly scattered. Also expose a heuristic to prefer kernels that minimize kernel-launch count for the expected token length distribution.
3) Prefill Prioritization & Locality-aware Eviction: prefetch high-score fragments during prefill step up to a budget (bytes/req). Eviction will prefer fragments with lowest reuse score but prefer evicting non-contiguous fragments first (to reduce fragmentation). A background compaction pass can opportunistically coalesce low-use fragments into contiguous free regions during low load.

Design trade-offs considered: 
- Accuracy vs. overhead for reuse scoring: chose approximate counters to keep CPU cost small; alternative was full histograms (too heavy).
- Aggressive compaction reduces fragmentation but can increase transient CPU and memory churn; compaction will be rate-limited and can be disabled for real-time SLAs.
- Kernel selection heuristics are heuristics (not optimal); fallback behaviors ensure correctness.

Acceptance criteria: 
- Microbench: 95th percentile decode latency for long-chat workload (avg context 32k tokens) improves by >=12% on p4d equivalent nodes.
- Per-token GPU utilization increases (fewer kernel launches) measured by trace capture across 1000 requests.
- Prefill CPU overhead < 1.5% of baseline; memory overhead (metadata) < 0.5% of KV memory.
- Unit tests for score update logic, kernel selector behavior, and eviction policy.

Implementation plan: 
- Phase 1 (this ticket, 2 sprints): implement fragment reuse scoring, integrate with eviction ranking, and expose config knobs. Add unit tests and a benchmark harness.
- Phase 2 (follow-ups ENG-12877, ENG-12878): extend kernel selector to use contiguous-range heuristic; implement prefill prioritizer and background compaction.
- Phase 3: rollout behind runtime feature flag, enable on canary fleet, gather telemetry, iterate.

Instrumentation & telemetry: capture reuse score distribution, pages prefetched per request, kernel launch count per request, compaction operations/sec. Add dashboard widgets to runtime-ops console for these metrics.

Rollout notes: default behavior is no-op until feature flag enabled. Start internal canary (20% of internal cluster), monitor SLOs for increased latency or CPU. Gradually ramp to 100% after two weeks of stable metrics.

Security & compatibility: no customer data persists outside existing KV; scoring metadata stored in runtime memory only. No additional crypto required. Backwards-compatibility maintained: format on-disk unchanged, eviction only reorders pages.

Open questions: 
- Should the reuse window be configurable per-customer workload? Proposal: expose knob for Dedicated/Private customers and keep conservative defaults for hosted tiers.
- How to handle multi-model sharing of cache pages when quant variants of a model use the same keys? We propose a reuse-agnostic shared map as a later RFC.

Related artifacts: design doc (Drive): https://drive.redwood.ai/docs/fragment-aware-kernel-routing (internal), benchmark PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4132 (WIP).
